source.title: Over-Parameterization and Generalization in Audio Classification
source.authors: Khaled Koutini; Hamid Eghbalzadeh; Florian Henkel; Jan Schlüter; G. Widmer

record.file_problem: Text appears to contain the full paper, including appendices.
record.tranche_reason: The study trains audio CNNs on random labels and reports training accuracy, applying the claim’s central intervention in a new modality.
record.gate_note: The random-label training accuracies and the true-label baseline are reported in Section 4. The study does not report test error on random labels. Scaling results, pruning results, and effective receptive field measurements do not test the other claim versions.
record.test_reason: The study reports its own random-label training accuracies for acoustic-scene CNNs, testing V1 in an audio setting.
record.authors_conclusion: The record accurately paraphrases the local random-label result: W = 32 reaches 99.99% accuracy on true labels and 85.51% on random labels; W = 64 reaches 100% on random labels, which the authors interpret as over-parameterization. The paper's main conclusion is that widening improves generalization to unseen recording devices, even with fixed parameter counts, whereas increasing depth can worsen it.
record.recipe_differences: The study uses CNNs for audio classification and reports random-label training accuracy, extending the fitting test to audio models. It does not report random-label test error.
record.method_sensitivity: Width changes the reported random-label training accuracy: W = 32 gives 85.51%, while W = 64 gives 100%.
record.peer_reviewed: Presented at the ICML 2021 Workshop on Overparameterization: Pitfalls & Opportunities.
record.problems: Random-label test error is not reported. The paper reports the mean and standard deviation of the last 10 epochs across three runs for its experiments generally, but does not state uncertainty alongside the random-label accuracy figures.
record.rows_left_out: No other reported results bear directly on the listed claim versions.

untested.parts: Random-label test error is unreported. Appendix A gives a general training recipe, but does not explicitly confirm identical hyperparameters for the random-label and true-label experiments or describe the randomization procedure.
Relative training time and convergence as label corruption increases.
Fitting shuffled pixels, independently permuted pixels, or Gaussian-noise inputs.
Training and test performance across intermediate fractions of corrupted labels.

Effects of weight decay, dropout, and augmentation on random-label fitting, and generalization after removing regularization. The general augmentation recipe supplies no explicit regularization comparison.
The temporal ordering of learning real patterns and memorizing noisy labels.

record.verdict_notes: The study is not an original source for these versions. Width, pruning, and receptive-field results on true-label generalization do not independently test the listed random-label claims.

versions.untested_parts: The study does not report test error on random labels or establish that the random-label training accuracies were reached without changing training hyperparameters relative to the true-label setting.

rows.subject: baseline network with W = 32, D = 1, K = 1
rows.operation_detail: Trained on the training data with random labels.
rows.note: The paper states this network can fit the training data with random labels to 85.51% accuracy.
rows.check: The value is correct: 85.51% training accuracy leaves 14.49% error, substantially short of near-zero error.

source_check.locator_found: Section 4, lines 248–251: W=32, D=1, K=1; random-label training accuracy 85.51%.

rows.check: The value is correct. This is a wider architecture than R1; it establishes perfect random-label fitting at W = 64, not at the W = 32 baseline.

source_check.locator_found: Section 4, lines 250–252: same network with W=64 achieves 100% random-label training accuracy.

rows.subject: baseline network with W = 32, D = 1, K = 1
